G8705.d: the commander of fifty men , (Xenophon Historicus) (ML)

G8708.d: 1. fiftieth , (Plato Philosophus) 2. as Substantive, ἡ πεντηκοστή, 3. (i.e. μερίς); at Athens the duty of one-fiftieth , or two per century , on all exports and imports, (Isaeus Orator); εὕρηκε καινὴν ἱππικῆς τινὰ πεντηκοστήν he invented a new two per century duty , in lieu of his cavalry service, i. e. paid this instead of it, (Demosthenes Orator) 4. (i.e. ἡμέρα); the fiftieth day (after the Passover), Pentecost , (New Testament) (ML)

G8709.d: 1. ripe , Lat. maturus, [variant datesAnthology Palantina 2. metaphorically softened , ὀργή (Sophocles Tragicus) (ML)

G8711.d: 1. of fruit, cooked by the sun, ripe, mellow , Lat. mitis, (Herdotus Historicus), etc. 2. metaphorically in vocative, mostly as a term of endearment, kind, gentle , ὦ πέπον my good friend , (Iliad by Homer); κριὲ πέπον my pet ram, (Odyssey by Homer);—; in bad sense, soft, weak , (Iliad by Homer); ὦ πέπονες ye weaklings , (Iliad by Homer): —; μόχθος πέπων softened pain, (Sophocles Tragicus), etc.: with dative, ἐχθροῖς π. gentle to one's foes, (Aeschulus Tragicus) (ML)

G8712.d: 1. to bring to an end, finish, accomplish, execute , [variant datesTragica Adespota, etc.:—;Pass. to be brought to an end, be finished , πάντα πεπείρανται (Odyssey by Homer): to be fulfilled, accomplished , (Euripides) etc. 2. in speaking, to end a discourse, finish speaking, (Aeschulus Tragicus), etc. 3. to repeat from beginning to end , (Aristophanes Comicus):—; to relate , (Euripides) 4. absolute to effect one's purpose , especially with a negative, οὐδὲν π. to come to no issue, do no good, make no progress , (Euripides) 5. intransitive to make way, reach or penetrate , (Aeschulus Tragicus) 6. intransitive to come to an end, end , (Plutarch) (ML)

G8717.d: looked at from all sides, admired of all observers , (Euripides) (ML)

G8719.d: 1. anything which is thrown round, a covering , (Plato Philosophus); χειρῶν περιβολαί embraces , (Euripides); so περιβολαί alone, (Xenophon Historicus); περιβολαὶ χθονός, i. e. the grave, (Euripides); π. [ ξίφεος] a scabbard, (Euripides): absolute of walls round a town, ἑπτάπυργοι π. (Euripides) 2. a space enclosed, compass , οἰκίης μεγάλης περιβολή a house of large compass , (Herdotus Historicus) 3. a circumference, circuit , (Thucydides); π. ποιεῖσθαι to make a circuit , (Xenophon Historicus) 4. metaphorically, 5. a compassing, endeavouring after , τῆς ἀρχῆς, Lat. affectatio imperii, (Xenophon Historicus) 6. ἡ π. τοῦ λόγου the whole compass of the matter, long and short of it, (Isocrates Orator) (ML)

G8720.d: 1. going round, compassing, encircling , (Euripides) 2. as Substantive, περίβολος = περιβολή, ἐχίδνης περίβολοι the spires or coils of a serpent, (Euripides); in plural walls round a town , (Herdotus Historicus); so in singular, (Thucydides) 3. an enclosure, circuit, compass , π. νεωρίων (Euripides); of a temple, the precincts , (Plutarch) (ML)

G8723.d: 1. with two right hands , i.e. using both hands alike , (Iliad by Homer) 2. very dexterous , (Aristophanes Comicus) (ML)

G8724.d: Dep. to grasp a thing with the hand , with genitive rei, (Plutarch) (ML)

G8725.d: 1. to be around a place, with dative, (Thucydides); τὰ περιόντα circumstances , (Demosthenes Orator) 2. to be better than, superior to another, surpass, excel , with genitive, (Iliad by Homer); περίεσσι γυναικῶν εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε (Odyssey by Homer); οἳ περὶ μὲν βουλὴν Δαναῶν περὶ δd ἐστὲ μάχεσθαι λπαρr εθυαλσs μάχην)) (Iliad by Homer); with dative rei, σοφίᾳ π. τῶν Ἑλλήνων (Plato Philosophus): absolute to be superior , (Herdotus Historicus), etc.; ἐκ περιόντος at an advantage , (Thucydides) 3. to overlive, outlive , τινι (Herdotus Historicus): absolute to survive, remain alive , (Herdotus Historicus), etc.:—;of things, to be extant, to be in existence , (Herdotus Historicus) 4. to be over and above, to remain in hand , of property, money, etc., (Thucydides); οἰόμενοι περιεῖναι χρήματά τῳ imagining that any one has a balance in his hands, (Demosthenes Orator) 5. to be a result or consequence , περίεστιν ὑμῖν ἐκ τούτων what you have got by all this is . ., (Demosthenes Orator); τοσοῦτον ὑμῖν περίεστιν τοῦ πρὸς ἐμὲ μίσους you have so much hatred against me left , Philipp. quoted in (Demosthenes Orator); with infinitive, περίεστι ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς ἐρίζειν it remains for you to quarrel with them, (Demosthenes Orator) (ML)

G8726.d: a girdle round the loins, apron , (Plutarch) (ML)

G8730.d: to be seated or to sit all round , (Herdotus Historicus): of an army, to beleaguer, invest a town, (Herdotus Historicus); of ships, to blockade , (Herdotus Historicus): with accusative pers. to sit down by one, (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G8732.d: to shear or clip all round , (Herdotus Historicus); Mid., περικείρεσθαι τρίχας to have one's hair clipt , (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G8736.d: 1. to seize around, embrace , (Xenophon Historicus) 2. to encompass or surround an enemy, so as to intercept him, (Herdotus Historicus); μετεώρους τὰς ναῦς π. to intercept them at sea, (Thucydides); ἐπεὰν δὲ αὐτὸν περιλάβῃς when you get hold of him, catch him, (Herdotus Historicus):—;Pass. to be caught , οἴμοι, περιείλημμαι μόνος (Aristophanes Comicus) 3. to comprehend, include , of a number of particulars, (Isocrates Orator) (ML)

G8740.d: to go all round , with accusative, (Plutarch) (ML)

G8741.d: 1. a going round, a flank march , (Herdotus Historicus) 2. a way round, the circumference, circuit, compass , τοῦ τείχεος, τῆς λίμνης (Herdotus Historicus); absolute, τὴν π. in circumference , (Herdotus Historicus) 3. γῆς π. a chart or map of the earth (compare πίναξ); (Herdotus Historicus) 4. a going round in a circle, circuit , (Plutarch) 5. of Time, a cycle or period of time , (Pindar), etc. 6. a prescribed course of life, system , (Plato Philosophus) 7. a fit of intermittent fever, (Demosthenes Orator) 8. = περιφορά, a course at dinner , (Xenophon Historicus); π. λόγων table-talk , (Xenophon Historicus) 9. the orbit of a heavenly body , (Xenophon Historicus) 10. a well-rounded sentence, period , (Aristotle Philosopher) (ML)

G8742.d: 1. to build round , (Demosthenes Orator) 2. to enclose by building round , (Demosthenes Orator):—;Pass. to be built up, walled in , (Thucydides); τὸ περιοικοδομημένον the space built round, the enclosure , Lat. ovile, (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G8745.d: 1. a walking about, walking , (Plato Philosophus), etc. 2. a place for walking, a covered walk , (Xenophon Historicus) 3. discourse during a walk, a philosophical discussion , (Aristophanes Comicus) 4. οἱ ἐκ τοῦ περιπάτου the Peripatetics, school of Aristotle , because he taught walking in a περίπατος of the Lyceum at Athens, (Plutarch), etc. (ML)

G8746.d: 1. to twine or enfold round :—;Pass. to fold oneself round , with dative, ἱστῷ περιπλεχθείς (Odyssey by Homer); absolute, δίκτυον εὖ μάλα περιπλεκόμενον close folding , (Xenophon Historicus) 2. to complicate, entangle , (Lucian) 3. to wrap up in words , (Aeschines Orator) (ML)

G8747.d: a station for περίπολοι, a guard-house , (Thucydides) (ML)

G8748.d: edged with purple , π. ἐσθής a robe with a purple border , the Roman toga praetextata or laticlavia , (Polybius Historicus), etc. (ML)

G8751.d: to besprinkle all round , especially in sacred rites:—;Mid. to purify oneself , (Theophrastus Philosophus) (ML)

G8753.d: dry and hard all round, exceeding hard , of iron, (Sophocles Tragicus):—;metaphorically obstinate, stubborn , (Sophocles Tragicus) (ML)

G8757.d: 1. a standing round, a crowd standing round , Lat. corona, (Theophrastus Philosophus), etc. 2. circumstances, a state of affairs , (Polybius Historicus):—;in bad sense, κατὰ τὰς π. in critical times , (Polybius Historicus) 3. outward pomp and circumstance , (Polybius Historicus) (ML)

G8758.d: 1. to dress, clothe, wrap up , (Pindar); ἔπηξα δ᾽ αὐτὸν εὖ περιστείλας I planted the sword having wrapt it well with earth , i. e. planted it firmly , (Sophocles Tragicus) 2. to dress or lay out a corpse, Lat. componere, (Odyssey by Homer), attic: simply, to bury , (Plato Philosophus) 3. metaphorically to wrap up, cloak, cover , τἄδικ᾽ εὖ π. (Euripides):—;Mid., τὰ σὰ περιστέλλου κακά (Euripides) 4. to take care of, protect, defend , (Herdotus Historicus); π. τοὺς νόμους to maintain the laws, (Herdotus Historicus); τὰ πάτρια (Demosthenes Orator); π. ἀοιδάν to uphold minstrelsy, (Pindar) (ML)

G8762.d: 1. to whirl round , of one preparing to throw, (Homer); π. ἵππον to wheel it round , (Plutarch):—; Pass. to be turned round, spin round , (Iliad by Homer); π. εἰς τἀληθῆ to come round to it, (Plato Philosophus) 2. π. τὼ χεῖρε to tie his hands behind him, (Lysias Orator). (ML)

G8763.d: 1. with pillars round the wall, surrounded with a colonnade , (Herdotus Historicus) 2. as Substantive, περίστυλον, ου, τό, or περίστυλος, ὁ, a peristyle, colonnade round a temple or court-yard , (Plutarch) (ML)

G8764.d: 1. to drag about , ἄνω καὶ κάτω (Lucian) 2. to tear away from , τί τινος (Polybius Historicus) (ML)

G8765.d: 1. to slit and tear off , (Plutarch) 2. Pass., of a river, περισχίζεσθαι τὸν χῶρον to split round a piece of land, i. e. split into two branches so as to surround it, (Herdotus Historicus);—;so, of a stream of men, to part and go different ways , (Plato Philosophus) (ML)

G8766.d: 1. to wall all round , πλίνθοις Βαβυλῶνα (Aristophanes Comicus) 2. to surround with a wall , so as to beleaguer, (Thucydides) 3. to build round , ὁ περιτετειχισμένος κύκλος (Xenophon Historicus) (ML)

G8768.d: 1. the line round a circular body, a periphery, circumference , (Aristotle Philosopher) 2. the outer surface , (Plutarch) 3. a round body , (Plutarch) from περιφερής (ML)

G8769.d: 1. moving round, surrounding , with genitive, (Euripides) 2. surrounded by , with dative, (Euripides) 3. round, circular , (Plato Philosophus):—;of bodies, spherical, globular , (Plato Philosophus):—;of style, rounded , (Aristotle Philosopher) (ML)

G8770.d: 1. meats carried round , (Xenophon Historicus) 2. a going round, rotatory motion, circuit, revolution , (Aristophanes Comicus), etc. 3. the revolving vault of heaven, (Plato Philosophus) 4. metaphorically, ἐν ταῖς περιφοραῖς in society , (Plutarch) (ML)

G8773.d: to surround with a stockade , (Aeschines Orator) (ML)

G8774.d: exceeding joyous or glad , (Herdotus Historicus), etc.; τινι at a thing, (Herdotus Historicus):—; τὸ π. excessive joy , (Thucydides) (ML)

G8775.d: to pour round or over , τί τινι, properly of liquids, (Homer); of metal-workers, χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας having spread gold leaf round its horns, (Iliad by Homer); so in Mid., ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε τις χρυσὸν περιχεύεται ἀργύρῳ (Odyssey by Homer):—;Pass. to be poured around , περὶ δ᾽ ἀμβρόσιος κέχυθ᾽ ὕπνος (Iliad by Homer); τῶν ὀστέων περικεχυμένων heaped all round , (Herdotus Historicus); of persons, περιχυθέντες crowding round , (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G8778.d: 1. to soften, ripen or change , by means of heat: 2. of the sun, to ripen fruit, (Odyssey by Homer); compare πεπαίνω. 3. by the action of fire, to cook, dress, bake , (Herdotus Historicus):—;Pass., (Herdotus Historicus):—;Mid., πέσσεσθαι πέμματα to cook oneself cakes, (Herdotus Historicus) 4. of the stomach, to digest , like Lat. concoquere, (Aristotle Philosopher) 5. metaphorically, χόλον πέσσειν to cherish or nurse one's wrath, Lat. fovere, (Iliad by Homer); βέλος πέσσειν to have a dart in one to nurse , (Iliad by Homer); but in good sense, γέρα πεσσέμεν to enjoy them, (Iliad by Homer); also, ἀκίνδυνον αἰῶνα πέσσειν to lead a sodden life of ease, (Pindar) (ML)

G8779.d: 1. a leaf , mostly in plural, (Homer):—; poetry, νεικέων πέταλα contentious votes (compare πεταλισμός); (Pindar) 2. a leaf of metal , (Lucian) (ML)

G8780.d: to spread out sails or clothes, (Odyssey by Homer); χεῖρε πετάσσας, of one swimming, (Odyssey by Homer): metaphorically, θυμὸν πετάσαι to open one's heart, (Odyssey by Homer):—;Pass., mostly in perfect, to be spread on all sides , (Homer): participle spread wide, opened wide , of folding doors, πύλαι πεπταμέναι (Iliad by Homer); πετάσθησαν (Odyssey by Homer) (ML)

G8781.d: a perch for fowls to roost at night, (Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus) derivation uncertain (ML)

G8783.d: 1. throwing stones , (Xenophon Historicus) 2. as Substantive, πετροβόλος, an engine for throwing stones , Lat. ballista, (Polybius Historicus), etc. (ML)

G8784.d: 1. the pine , (Iliad by Homer), etc. 2. any thing made from its wood, a torch of pine-wood , [variant datesTragica Adespota 3. a writing-tablet , (Euripides) (ML)

G8785.d: of or from pine or pine-wood , (Sophocles Tragicus); π. δάκρυα tears of the pine , i. e. the resinous drops that ooze from it, (Euripides) (ML)

G8787.d: 1. anything joined together, framework , of a ship, [variant datesAnthology Palantina:—;Lat. pegma, a moveable scaffold used in theatres, (Juvenal) 2. metaphorically, π. γενναίως παγέν a bond in honour bound, (Aeschulus Tragicus) 3. π. τῆς χιόνος frozen snow, (Polybius Historicus) (ML)

G8788.d: 1. to leap, spring, bound , ὑψόσε ποσσὶν ἐπήδα (Iliad by Homer); π. ἐς σκάφος (Sophocles Tragicus); with accusative cognate, πήδημα πηδᾶν to take a leap, (Euripides); with accusative loci, πεδία πηδᾶν to bound over them, (Sophocles Tragicus); π. πλάκα (Euripides) 2. metaphorically of an arrow, (Iliad by Homer); of the heart, to leap, throb , (Aristophanes Comicus), etc.; of sudden changes, τί πηδᾶις εἰς ἄλλους τρόπου; (Euripides) (ML)

G8789.d: of clay , Lat. fictilis, οἱ πήλινοι clay figures , (Demosthenes Orator) (ML)

G8790.d: 1. to make fat, fatten , (Euripides); π. χθόνα to fatten the soil, of a dead man, (Aeschulus Tragicus):—;Pass. to be or become fat , (Plato Philosophus), etc. 2. metaphorically, 3. to increase, enlarge , πλοῦτον (Pindar) 4. to make wanton, excite , (Aeschulus Tragicus): —;Pass. to wax fat and wanton , (Aeschulus Tragicus); ἔχθεσιν πιαίνεσθαι to batten on quarrels, (Pindar) (ML)

G8791.d: an ape, monkey , (Aristophanes Comicus); as feminine, πίθηκος μήτηρ (Babrius Fabularum Scriptor):—;of persons, an ape, jackanapes , (Aristophanes Comicus) derivation uncertain (ML)

G8792.d: πιθός, see: πειθός. πειθός (πιθός, WH), -ή, -όν (πείθω), = cl. πιθανός, persuasive: 1Co.2:4 (not found elsewhere).† (AS)

G8796.d: pitch , Lat. pix, (Iliad by Homer), etc.: proverbial, ἄρτι μῦς πίττης γεύεται, i. e. he has got the first taste of misery, (Demosthenes Orator) (ML)

G8797.d: the pine, stone pine , (Homer):—;proverbial, πίτυος τρόπον ἐκτρίβεσθαι to be destroyed like a pine , i. e. utterly , because the pine when cut down never grows again, (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G8798.d: 1. neuter πῖον, genitive πίονος, fat, plump , Lat. pinguis, (Homer); π. δημός rich fat, (Iliad by Homer); of oil, (Herdotus Historicus) 2. of soil, fat, rich. (Iliad by Homer); also, πίονα ἔργα pingues segetes , (Iliad by Homer); ὀπώρας πίων ποτός, of wine, (Sophocles Tragicus) 3. of persons and places, rich, wealthy , (Homer); πίονι μέτρῳ in plenteous measure, (Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus) 4. The comparative and Sup. are πι-ότερος, πι-ότατος, as if from πῖος. (ML)

G8799.d: to turn sideways or aside , πλ. πρὸς τοὺς ἀντίους ἀνέμους (i.e. τὴν ναῦν); to beat up against adverse winds, (Lucian): metaphorically, πλ. ἢ φωνὴν ἢ πρᾶξιν to adapt them to circumstances , (Plutarch) (ML)
